content: 1. If a Community Health Centre (CHC) already exists, efforts should be directed towards integrating palliative care services into its current offerings. However, it is crucial to ensure that this does not overburden the existing staff unless additional personnel are hired or their current responsibilities are reduced. Advocacy efforts can highlight the cost savings associated with palliative care, such as reduced hospital admissions and shorter lengths of stay. 2. The medical and ethical importance of palliative care should be communicated to CHC staff to gain their support. It must be emphasized that these services will not add to their workload unnecessarily. 3. Training should initially focus on the medical doctors, clinical officers, or assistant doctors at the CHC. They should receive at least 35 hours of combined theoretical and practical training in basic palliative care. Once trained, these medical professionals can assist in training nurses and community health workers or volunteers. At least one nurse, preferably two, at each CHC should also undergo 35 hours of training in basic palliative nursing care. These trained nurses and doctors can then help train community health workers or volunteers. Existing community health workers with some home-care training should receive 3–6 hours of additional training to identify and report uncontrolled physical, psychological, or social distress to a supervisor at the CHC. New volunteers can be trained using a 16-hour curriculum. 4. At a minimum, CHCs should provide outpatient palliative care services. They can also support home care by supervising community health workers or volunteers, sending nursing or medical staff for home visits as needed, or maintaining contact with patients and families via mobile phones. CHCs with inpatient beds can offer uncomplicated end-of-life care for one or two patients at a time if families are unable to provide care at home. This care at a CHC is significantly less expensive than hospital care. 5. Establishing a new community-based palliative care service often requires a step-by-step approach. The first step involves conducting awareness meetings for individuals and organizations interested in helping incurably ill patients. Volunteers willing to dedicate time weekly should be registered. A social support program can be initiated with these volunteers to address needs such as food for starving families, educational support for patients' children, and emotional support for patients and families. 6. Volunteers should be trained using a standardized 16-hour curriculum that includes basic nursing care, communication skills, and emotional support. Weekly review meetings should be held to discuss solutions to documented problems. Volunteers can also document the issues faced by incurably ill patients in their neighborhoods. 7. A nursing component should be added to the program. This may involve hiring a part-time nurse or encouraging a local nurse to undergo palliative care training. Nurse-led home-care programs can be initiated, and in some cases, nursing assistance may be available from nearby palliative care units. A culture of meticulous documentation and review should be established. 8. Adding a medical component is often challenging due to the scarcity of trained doctors. Local doctors can be encouraged to undergo palliative care training, and self-study can be supported with relevant reading materials. The health system must ensure the training of specialized personnel. 9. Once a home-care service is established, a regular outpatient clinic can be considered. However, this requires more resources and funding than a home-care service. A trained doctor and nurse are prerequisites for the clinic, which can often be linked to a local hospital. 10. A system of regular review and evaluation should be established to identify areas for improvement. Palliative care services often receive appreciation from the community, but complacency must be avoided. 11. The Kerala Neighborhood Network in Palliative Care (NNPC) in India serves as a model for community-led palliative care. It emphasizes community ownership, with funding sourced from small community donations and strong media and political support. The program has been replicated in other regions of India and internationally, such as in Jakarta, Indonesia. The NNPC model is based on community participation facilitated by civil society, religious organizations, local governments, and political parties. 12. Hospital-based palliative care services should be available in all hospitals treating cancer patients and those with chronic diseases like HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory diseases, heart failure, and chronic renal diseases. These services improve patient outcomes by providing comprehensive care, facilitating discussions about care goals, and reducing hospital stays and non-beneficial treatments near the end of life. 13. Hospital-based palliative care services can include outpatient clinics, inpatient consultation services, day-care services, inpatient palliative care units, and outreach/home-care services. Outpatient clinics are cost-effective and can be expanded later. Inpatient consultation services can build the capacity of other staff in pain management and palliative care. Day-care services can provide symptom stabilization, caregiver respite, and counseling. Inpatient palliative care units offer consistent care and serve as training hubs. Outreach services bring care to patients unable to travel, leveraging family caregivers' strengths. 14. Setting up a hospital-based palliative care service involves conducting a needs assessment, defining priorities, and identifying a target population. The service should initially focus on terminal cancer patients and gradually expand to include all patients with serious, chronic, life-limiting conditions. The hospital must ensure the availability of essential palliative care medicines, particularly oral morphine, and provide accessible facilities for patients and their families.
